Name: Priene Inscription of Alexander the Great
Short Description: A short dedication from the Temple of Athena Polias at Priene stating that “King Alexander dedicated the temple to Athena Polias.” Probably set up around Alexander’s campaign in Ionia in 334 BCE, it records royal patronage of a prominent civic sanctuary and publicly associates Alexander’s kingship with the city’s cult of Athena.

Name: On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Becoming (Process Ontology)
Short Description: A mathematical-astronomical treatise using geometry and observation to estimate the relative sizes and distances of the Sun, Moon, and Earth. Aristarchus concludes that the Sun is much larger and farther away than the Moon and that the Earth is larger than the Moon. The surviving work itself uses an Earth-centered geometric setup; Aristarchus’ heliocentric hypothesis is known from other ancient testimony. Its importance lies in its quantitative mathematical treatment of astronomy.

Name: Dedication to Attalos I at Herakleia near Latmos
Arts and Sciences Tags: Political Science / Law, Public Relations, History
Short Description: A fragmentary marble altar inscription naming King Attalos Soter, identified with Attalos I of Pergamon. The dedication probably belongs to his reign and may date particularly to the 230s BCE, when Pergamene power temporarily extended into Caria. Though extremely brief, it provides direct evidence for the local honoring of Attalos beyond Pergamon.

Name: Teos Grants Land to the Dionysiac Artists
Short Description: A civic decree granting the Dionysiac Artists of Ionia and the Hellespont a property in or near Teos, purchased by the city for 6,000 drachmas and dedicated to the guild as tax-free sacred property. The decree also orders civic officials to include prayers for the organization’s success. It documents the close link between Teos, the professional association of performers, and the civic cult of Dionysus.

Name: Antiochus III Letter to Sardis
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle)
Arts and Sciences Tags: Political Science / Law, Public Relations, History
Short Description: The surviving end of a royal letter from Antiochus III to Sardis, dated to 213 BCE. It orders measures connected with the city’s synoecism, releases Sardis from an additional one-twentieth tax, and restores its former gymnasium, while referring implementation to royal officials including Zeuxis and Ktesikles. The letter illustrates Seleucid rule through negotiated fiscal relief, civic restoration, and administrative oversight.

Name: Parian Decree Accepting the Games of Artemis Leukophryene
Short Description: A decree of Paros accepting Magnesia on the Maeander’s invitation to the quadrennial games of Artemis Leukophryene, around 207/6 BCE. Paros recognizes Magnesia and its territory as sacred and inviolable, accepts the sacrifice and crown games as equivalent in status to the Pythian games, and provides for official participation. The inscription documents how cult, festival recognition, and inter-polis diplomacy reinforced one another.

Short Description: A late-Hellenistic dossier from Pergamon regulating the cult of Athena Nikephoros. It combines rules concerning ritual purity and access to the sanctuary with civic decrees governing sacrificial dues and the handling of revenues such as animal skins. The text shows civic institutions and sanctuary administration jointly codifying ritual practice and cult finances in post-Attalid Pergamon.

Name: Conics
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism), Monism (Single Principle)
Arts and Sciences Tags: Mathematics, Logic / Formal Reasoning, Philosophy, Art / Aesthetics
Short Description: Apollonius of Perga’s systematic study of the ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola as sections of a cone. The work comprised eight books: Books I–IV survive in Greek, Books V–VII principally through Arabic transmission, and Book VIII is lost. Its rigorous terminology, constructions, and proofs made it the most comprehensive ancient treatment of conic sections and a major influence on later geometry and mathematical astronomy.
Author: Apollonius of Perga

Name: Decree on the Festival of Zeus Sosipolis
Short Description: A civic decree from Magnesia on the Maeander regulating the festival and sacrifice of Zeus Sosipolis, “Savior of the City.” It provides for the annual dedication of a bull at the sowing season, public prayers for peace and agricultural abundance, a procession, sacrifices to Zeus Sosipolis and other deities, and civic funding and participation. The text closely integrates municipal administration, agricultural well-being, and public cult.

Name: Honorific Decrees for Moschion, Krates, and Zosimos
Metaphysical Tags: Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Dialectics (Conflict)
Arts and Sciences Tags: Political Science / Law, Public Relations, History
Short Description: A modern grouping of separate late-Hellenistic honorific decrees from Priene. Moschion, honored after 129 BCE, is praised for a long career of civic benefaction and public service; Krates was honored around 89 BCE for civic advocacy and magistracies; and Zosimos was honored around 80 BCE in several decrees for service including the gymnasiarchy, stephanephorate, and secretaryship. Together the inscriptions document euergetism, diplomacy, and civic government as Priene adapted to expanding Roman power.

Name: Nemrut Dağ Inscriptions of Antiochus I
Metaphysical Tags: Becoming (Process Ontology), Pluralism (Multiplicities), Grid (Systematic Structuralism), Clockwork (Causal Determinism)
Arts and Sciences Tags: Political Science / Law, Public Relations, History
Short Description: Monumental Greek cult inscriptions associated with Antiochus I of Commagene’s sanctuary at Nemrut Dağ. They regulate festivals and priestly duties, articulate the king’s dynastic cult, and pair Greek and Iranian divine names such as Zeus-Oromasdes, Apollo-Mithras-Helios-Hermes, and Artagnes-Herakles-Ares. The inscriptions also connect Antiochus to claimed Persian and Seleucid-Macedonian ancestry, using religious syncretism and genealogy to frame royal legitimacy.
